content: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency in the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase, which is necessary for the proper metabolism of phenylalanine, an amino acid. In individuals with PKU, dietary restriction of phenylalanine is the primary method to maintain low blood phenylalanine levels. This dietary approach involves the exclusion of most natural foods, with supplementation used to provide essential nutrients. Recent studies have reported that treatment with sapropterin dihydrochloride, a synthetic form of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), can reduce blood phenylalanine levels in some patients with PKU. This review aimed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of sapropterin dihydrochloride in lowering blood phenylalanine concentrations in individuals with PKU. The review is an update of a previously published Cochrane Review. To identify relevant studies, researchers searched the Inborn Errors of Metabolism Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and Current Controlled Trials databases. The last searches were conducted on August 11, 2014, and September 4, 2014, respectively. Additionally, the drug manufacturer, BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc., was contacted for information on any unpublished trials. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared sapropterin treatment with either no supplementation or placebo in individuals with PKU caused by phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency. Two authors independently assessed the trials and extracted data on outcomes. Two placebo-controlled trials met the inclusion criteria. The first trial involved 89 children and adults with PKU who had previously demonstrated responsiveness to sapropterin. Participants received 10 mg/kg/day of sapropterin without dietary restrictions. The primary outcome measured was the change in blood phenylalanine concentration. The second trial screened 90 children aged 4 to 12 years with PKU who were on a restricted diet to determine their responsiveness to sapropterin. Of these, 46 responders entered the placebo-controlled phase of the trial and received 20 mg/kg/day of sapropterin. This trial measured changes in both blood phenylalanine concentration and protein tolerance. Both trials also reported adverse events. The trials were assessed to have an overall low risk of bias, although both were sponsored by BioMarin. In the first trial, the sapropterin group (10 mg/kg/day) showed a significant reduction in blood phenylalanine levels, with a mean difference of -238.80 μmol/L (95% confidence interval: -343.09 to -134.51). In the second trial, the group receiving 20 mg/kg/day of sapropterin showed a non-significant reduction in blood phenylalanine levels, with a mean difference of -51.90 μmol/L (95% confidence interval: -197.27 to 93.47). However, this trial reported a significant increase in protein tolerance, with a mean difference of 18.00 mg/kg/day (95% confidence interval: 12.28 to 23.72) in the sapropterin group. The authors concluded that there is evidence of short-term benefits from sapropterin treatment in individuals with sapropterin-responsive forms of PKU. These benefits include a reduction in blood phenylalanine levels and an increase in protein tolerance. No serious adverse events were associated with short-term sapropterin use. However, there is currently no evidence regarding the long-term effects of sapropterin, and its effectiveness in severe forms of PKU remains unclear.
